title: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
desc: Shifts attention from announcements to workflow fit, renewal economics, consumption costs and control of lawyers’ working environment.

kps.k: The cluster shifts the debate from AI announcements to the organisational work needed to turn tools into value.
kps.d: Atena Reyhani argues that firms must align capabilities with practical needs, deploy strategically, train users and manage change at scale. Nikki Shaver distinguishes licensing and rollout from sustained use, challenging the assumption that an approachable chat interface makes adoption automatic. She cites unspecified studies reporting roughly 70% firm-wide rollout among AmLaw 100 firms but adoption around 25%; missing definitions and methods prevent treating these as directly comparable measures. The substantive proposition is that workflow fit and organisational readiness—not product availability alone—determine practical uptake.

qs.q: And that is, number one, really aligning these capabilities of AI to practical organizations needs and being able to operationalize it at the scale to translate technology to value.
qs.a: The Evolution of AI in Legal Tech: A Conversation with ContractPodAi's Atena Reyhani · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: So recent studies have indicated that although approximately 70 % of the AmLaw 100  firms have rolled out some form of generative AI firm-wide, adoption rates of that technology hover around 25%.
qs.a: Fighting for Your Light: Anusia Gillespie on AI, Legal Innovation, and the Soul Toll of Law · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: Market inventories show expanding product coverage, not equivalent growth in adoption, performance or economic value.
kps.d: Legal Technology Hub reports about 400 generative-AI offerings in its early-2025 inventory, 855 product placements from 682 vendors at December 2025, and around 1,000 placements by March 2026. Wilkins explains that discovering previously unrecorded companies and features contributed to growth. Shaver also observes a late-2025 shift from broad assistants toward intake, operations, compliance and governance. These observations underpin her rejection of a fringe-technology narrative, but cannot establish market revenue, investment sustainability or successful deployment. Repeated map updates and promotional segments describe the same tracking effort rather than independent corroboration.

qs.q: And so we published that in the beginning of March and we got such an overwhelming response, either from companies we didn’t know about or companies who had Gen.AI features that we didn’t know about, that we decided to rush and do another update to the map just two weeks later to coincide with Legal Week.
qs.a: The Six-Minute Dilemma: Litera's Avaneesh Marwaha on Building Legal Tech That Actually Gets Used The Geek in Review · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: And it has 855 generative AI product placements by 682 vendors across 19 categories, which is obviously a massive landscape now.
qs.a: From Legal Aid to LIT Lab: Quinten Steenhuis and the Builder’s Approach to AI · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Procurement increasingly centres on demonstrated workflow fit, readiness and renewal value rather than buying first and finding uses later.
kps.d: Sam Moore describes stakeholder interviews, needs assessments and team-level sprints that identify use cases, refine workflows and sometimes reveal gaps between management expectations and lawyers' readiness. Renewal reviews examine where tools do and do not generate value. Cheryl Wilson-Griffin recommends structured demonstrations covering current customer use, references, integrations, security, onboarding and long-term support. Shaver stresses that mid-sized firms differ substantially by practice and resources, so a single adoption approach will not fit them all. Much of this material promotes LTH's advisory services, scorecards and education: it establishes a proposed process, not independently demonstrated effectiveness or impartiality.

qs.q: And sometimes those sprints reveal really interesting differences between management perception and attorneys’ actual readiness, which can be really valuable.
qs.a: Greg Mazares Sr. on AI, E-Discovery, and the Future of Human-Led Legal Services · AI-native providers · 2026

qs.q: You’re going to get very detailed questions on integrations, API, SOC 2, GDPR, regional data requirements.
qs.a: Law Librarians Take the Lead: The Future of AI and Legal Information · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Consumption pricing makes operational AI literacy a cost-control issue as well as a quality issue.
kps.d: Moore reports clients selecting the most sophisticated model and every optional feature regardless of task, then encountering slow responses and token limits. He also warns that large legal documents crowd context windows. In sponsor commentary, Wilkins reports Legora's Agent Pro move to consumption-based pricing and predicts wider adoption; she identifies repeated document uploads and prolonged conversations as potential cost drivers. These accounts support attention to model selection, context management and actual usage costs, but provide no quantified savings or accuracy tests. Shaver's account of Harvey's keynote adds that rising token consumption can reflect product complexity as well as adoption, making it an ambiguous usage indicator.

qs.q: I’ve seen law firm clients whose users just pick the most sophisticated model for everything, toggle on every optional feature available, and then are confused as to why responses are taking a long time and why they’re hitting token limits very, very quickly.
qs.a: LexisNexis CTO Greg Dickason on Agentic Legal AI, Protégé, Shepard’s Verify, and the Future of Legal Work · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: Recently, Legora also announced that it’s moving its Agent Pro offering to consumption-based pricing, which means it’s billing by what the agent does rather than by a flat seat license.
qs.a: From AI Personas to Rogue Agents: Rethinking Legal Training, Security, and Value · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: Competition concerns who controls lawyers' working environment, not just which model produces better answers.
kps.d: Claude's reported legal plugins and connectors, Midpage's Claude integration and other content partnerships raise the possibility that model providers become primary legal work platforms. Shaver envisages existing repositories feeding new working environments; the hosts ask whether general platforms complement or replace specialist applications. Niki Black predicts that large model providers could approach specialist legal quality through legal-data training and greater resources, while reporting strong disagreement from a legal-tech founder. Specialist fundraising and product announcements do not resolve that dispute. MCP offers a proposed integration route, but an unidentified Definely guest highlights a separate dependency: larger vendors may control access to the databases agents need.

qs.q: So if Claude is now launching legal practice area tools and connecting into major legal platforms through MCP, is Anthropic still just a model provider behind the scenes, or is it becoming a legal tech platform in its own right?
qs.a: Legal AI, Trust, and Agents: Joel Hron on Thomson Reuters, Anthropic, and the Future of CoCounsel · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: Now, maybe we’re thinking about something else as being the core system where you still have your data repositories, but they’re pushing into the system where lawyers will do their work.
qs.a: Pablo Arredondo and Joel Hron on Reasoning Models, Deep Research, and the Future of Legal AI · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: Agentic claims require scrutiny of actual autonomy, human control and enforceable governance.
kps.d: Shaver endorses Dan Hoadley's definition requiring tool use, reasoning, planning, adaptation and recognition of completion. A conference panel judged few products genuine agents under that definition, despite LTH mapping more than 100 offerings incorporating or announcing some form of agentic AI; different definitions and timing mean these claims are not directly contradictory. Shaver recommends asking whether lawyers can inspect and redirect plans before execution. Moore advocates readable, risk-differentiated policies rather than blanket prohibitions, while Shaver warns that having policies does not establish enforcement. Gebauer's intake questions—urgency, vulnerability, confidentiality and substantive assessment—illustrate why workflow automation requires more scrutiny than routine scheduling.

qs.q: True agents are able to come up with a plan about how to accomplish the overall goal, then pursue that plan and make adjustments to the plan during execution, and they will know when the overall goal is accomplished.
qs.a: Laura Clayton McDonnell on Legal Technology, AI, and Corporate Transformation at Thomson Reuters · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: A trend we’re seeing at the moment is a shift away from policies written in 2023 and 2024, which largely stated what you couldn’t do, and toward a more informative approach that defines different risk categories and makes distinctions between routine, low-risk uses of AI and other, more substantial use cases.
qs.a: Who Governs Big Tech? Hannah Bloch-Wehba on AI Regulation, Police Surveillance, and Public Accountability · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Knowledge quality and expert participation remain central to the proposed value of legal AI.
kps.d: Sam Flynn argues that sophisticated models and workflows cannot compensate for poor knowledge sources. He criticises generic retrieval tools that split clauses and lose document hierarchy, and describes Josef's development work without presenting performance measurements. Stephen Costigan offers a different architectural response: a firm-owned, internally hosted knowledge graph supporting research, drafting, review and search. Gebauer sees broader opportunities to combine internal documents with external and financial information. Together these claims move beyond faster document production toward usable institutional knowledge, while leaving comparative reliability and the productivity-versus-control trade-off untested.

qs.q: If you don’t get the knowledge source right, all of that is going to be for naught.
qs.a: RAG is Not Dead: Josef's Sam Flynn on Legal Tech That Works · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: I’ll start by saying our platform turns a firm’s documents and matter history into a private, curated knowledge graph that the firm owns and runs inside its own environment.
qs.a: Own the Graph: Stephen Costigan on Private AI, Knowledge Infrastructure, and Law Firm Advantage · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Forecasts differ over whether AI strengthens professional judgment or erodes the work through which lawyers develop and exercise it.
kps.d: Joel Hron predicts that difficult decisions and directing or correcting AI will occupy more of everyday work. Gregory Mostyn expects automated fact-finding to increase the importance of advocacy, storytelling and client context. Greg Dickason predicts faster associate development through simulated trials and depositions rather than junior elimination. Matt Samuels qualifies this optimism: excessive delegation could weaken strategic attention and legal craft, illustrated by a hypothetical exchange of maximal AI-generated redlines that prevents compromise. These accounts suggest training in both AI operation and substantive judgment, but supply no measured training, skill-retention or workforce outcomes. The ChatGPT retrospective is a model-generated interpretation of earlier interviews, not independent confirmation of guest agreement.

qs.q: It’s making these hard decisions, hard directions, hard re-steers of the AI model.
qs.a: Pablo Arredondo and Joel Hron on Reasoning Models, Deep Research, and the Future of Legal AI · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: And I think we’ll see AI helping us train junior associates, then being able to do mock trials and all the rest very quickly, mock depositions, all of that.
qs.a: LexisNexis CTO Greg Dickason on Agentic Legal AI, Protégé, Shepard’s Verify, and the Future of Legal Work · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: New delivery models and pricing possibilities do not establish a single employment or demand trajectory.
kps.d: Lambert attributes a Jevons-paradox argument to Filevine's guests: cheaper services could expand demand among previously priced-out users. Dickason similarly predicts broader service rather than fewer lawyers. Nori instead anticipates clients questioning Big Law spending and a profession divided between AI-enabled generalists and narrow human specialists. These forecasts concern different market segments and can coexist; none establishes net employment effects. Reported examples include Pierson Ferdinand's partner-only, AI-centred model and Garfield's small-business debt service. Shaver sees potential for workflow-based fees while retaining hours in AFA calculations; Andrew Thompson stresses hourly billing's resilience. Access to previously unmet legal help remains distinct from corporate savings or firm profitability.

qs.q: Many pundits out there are predicting that AI will contract the legal industry, but you guys are arguing the exact opposite of that using the Jevons paradox — the economic theory that technology makes resources cheaper and more efficient to produce, and then consumption actually skyrockets.
qs.a: Why AI Will Create More Legal Work, Not Less: Filevine's Rizner and Anderson on Research, Access, and Human Judgment · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: As clients understand how much AI tools can do, in-house teams will question why they’re hiring Big Law.
qs.a: Sateesh Nori Joins LawDroid: AI Tools for Access to Justice, Housing Court, and Legal Aid · Access to justice · 2026

vlens.an: Across this curated legal-tech-vendor voice, the substantive sources generally accept the proposition that product availability, funding and rollout do not by themselves establish realised value. Their common explanation is that value depends on practical workflow fit, strategic deployment, user training, change management, task-appropriate model use, cost control, reliable knowledge sources, integration and human oversight. The voice materially develops the proposition by offering concrete mechanisms: needs-led technology selection; modular implementation; source-linked verification; scrutiny of whether purported agents can plan and act; lawyer visibility into and control over agent plans; firm-owned knowledge infrastructure; and assessment of how model providers may control lawyers’ working environments. Material internal variation remains. Some excerpts merely catalogue products, funding or partnerships and therefore support only the expansion side of the proposition, while several promotional or introductory excerpts are too thin to establish a position. Other sources redirect toward prospective productivity, vendor education or AI-driven demand growth rather than realised procurement value. Forecasts also diverge over whether delegation will strengthen judgment and advocacy or erode legal craft. Claims about productivity, adoption effects and future market structure are mostly qualitative, promotional or predictive rather than measured; no supplied source clearly opposes the proposition.

qs.q: And that is, number one, really aligning these capabilities of AI to practical organizations needs and being able to operationalize it at the scale to translate technology to value.
qs.a: The Evolution of AI in Legal Tech: A Conversation with ContractPodAi's Atena Reyhani · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: For example, if an agent is operating in a legal workflow, you may want to know whether visibility has been built in so that you can see the plan the agent creates for achieving its overall goal before it gets going on that plan and whether the lawyer or user is able to course correct the plan before it is executed.
qs.a: Laura Clayton McDonnell on Legal Technology, AI, and Corporate Transformation at Thomson Reuters · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

vlens.an: The curated AI-native legal-provider sources support the proposition that legal-AI procurement should move beyond announcements and product availability toward everyday use, workflow fit, organisational readiness, due diligence and demonstrated renewal value. Their common reasoning is practical: firms and legal departments should identify specific use cases, compare products against operational and governance needs, test whether users are ready, and determine where an existing tool is actually generating business value before renewing substantial subscriptions. There is material variation in depth and emphasis. One source merely calls for attention to lawyers’ day-to-day use and supplies no adoption or economic evidence. The advisory source gives the strongest support through readiness assessments, workflow sprints and go/no-go renewal reviews, although these are observations from—and promotion of—advisory engagements rather than quantified proof of effectiveness. The Garfield AI discussion illustrates expansion into regulated, low-human-interaction legal-service delivery, while the accompanying product-comparison discussion stresses use-case fit, security, privacy and hosting; however, it offers no evidence of Garfield’s realised performance, adoption or affordability. Thus, these selected sources consistently accept the proposition’s core, but substantiate procurement processes and criteria more clearly than realised outcomes, consumption costs or control of lawyers’ working environment.

qs.q: And we’re finding that those AI enablement projects often lead into further work around AI procurement, which I think is a really encouraging sign that the industry is moving beyond the FOMO and the push to buy something now and  figure out how to use it later.
qs.a: Greg Mazares Sr. on AI, E-Discovery, and the Future of Human-Led Legal Services · AI-native providers · 2026

qs.q: So buyers can see the grid and assess relatively quickly which of the products is more likely to suit their individual needs.
qs.a: Philip Young of Garfield.AI: The World’s First AI Law Firm Gets the Green Light · AI-native providers · 2025

vlens.an: This curated Academia & research voice supports the proposition that legal AI’s expanding supply does not itself establish adoption, performance or realized value, and that attention should move toward workflow fit, procurement readiness and organisational governance. The clearest common reasoning is practical: buyers need structured evaluation, demonstrated use cases, integrations, onboarding, training and continuing support, while deployment requires readable, risk-differentiated policies and attention to compliance. Internal variation is material but complementary. Some sources provide concrete procurement processes spanning market analysis, evaluation frameworks, pilots and requirements; others document continuing vendor growth and a shift toward operational tools; governance-oriented sources foreground responsible organisational deployment; and the AI-centred-firm source treats business-model disruption as an open empirical question. The evidence is largely advisory, promotional or agenda-setting rather than measured research, so it supports the proposition’s caution more strongly than it demonstrates realized outcomes. It also says relatively little about renewal economics, consumption costs or control of lawyers’ working environments. The label should not be read as representing academia generally: several supplied excerpts report Legal Technology Hub practitioner commentary, and some introduced academic guests without including their substantive views.

qs.q: For each premium category, we have a landscape overview, an evaluation framework, a use case, a pilot guide, a requirements template, and then any other information we think is important.
qs.a: Lawyer 3.0 and the Milkshake Test: Ray Brescia on Legal AI, Client Value, and the Next Wave of Lawyering · Academia · 2026

qs.q: It’s like, well, what does it mean to responsibly deploy this to manage it within an organization?

vlens.an: This curated access-to-justice and civil-society selection supports the proposition that visible product expansion should not be equated with realised value. The substantive source documents a large and steadily expanding inventory of legal-AI offerings, but supplies no corresponding evidence on adoption, performance, revenue, renewals, workflow outcomes or improved access to justice. Its claims about reduced Big Law demand, professional polarisation and new service-delivery models are explicitly forecasts rather than observed effects. The second source reinforces the importance of implementation by promoting education on deployment and solution selection for mid-sized firms, but it is an event announcement rather than evidence that such deployment creates value. Material internal variation therefore lies in emphasis: one source combines market mapping with speculative profession-wide disruption, while the other focuses narrowly on practical training. Neither rejects the cluster’s procurement framing, although the first also redirects some attention toward service delivery, employment and systemic reform. Despite the access-to-justice framing, these excerpts do not demonstrate reduced unmet civil legal need or other access outcomes.

qs.q: It has 855 generative AI product placements by 682 vendors across 19 categories, which is obviously a massive landscape now.

vlens.an: This curated law-firm-practice evidence supports the proposition that expanding legal-AI supply does not itself establish adoption or realised value. The sources share a practical procurement orientation: one pairs reported growth in litigation products with the need for structured buyer evaluation, while the other argues that licensing tools may still yield weak adoption because workload, culture and organisational readiness obstruct changes in working practices. The principal internal variation is therefore one of emphasis rather than direction: product assessment and category selection in the first source, versus diagnosis of adoption barriers through stakeholder interviews, strategy and policy work in the second. Both remain practitioner or service-provider claims rather than independent evidence of improved uptake, workflow performance, renewal economics or case outcomes, and they should not be treated as representative of traditional law firms generally.

qs.q: These are collections of really in-depth content that allow buyers to review solutions in a particular category, evaluate them, provide the tools with which to evaluate solutions in that category.

qs.q: For example, in law firms, sometimes you might be in that moment where you’re trying to drive adoption of your AI initiatives, your AI tools that you’ve licensed, and it’s not going particularly well, and it can be hard to determine exactly why.

vlens.an: The curated market-analyst, consultancy and press sources generally accept the proposition that expanding legal-AI products and headline usage do not by themselves demonstrate realized value. Their common reasons are operational: workflow-specific fit, user capability, structured evaluation, governance and control, and the economic consequences of consumption-based pricing. They repeatedly distinguish observations, announcements and forecasts from measured adoption, performance, savings or renewal outcomes. Material variation remains. Some sources materially develop the proposition through concrete concerns about prompting-driven token costs, substantive safeguards for automated intake, knowledge synthesis and workflow-level pricing. Others are merely adjacent or evidentially thin, reporting survey figures, feature growth, conferences or market competition without addressing realized value. One redirects toward market structure, consolidation and access for smaller firms rather than procurement outcomes. This synthesis characterizes only the supplied curated sources and does not imply wider prevalence among market commentators.

qs.q: And what everyday prompting habits, from repasting whole documents to burying five questions in one prompt, might be driving up both cost and inaccuracy without you knowing it.

vlens.an: The supplied sources support the proposition that legal-AI procurement should be judged by realized operational value rather than product availability or headline price. Moore identifies task-insensitive model selection, context-window pressure, token limits and usage-based overages as mechanisms through which weak operational literacy can impair performance and raise actual costs. Wilson-Griffin complements this with a buyer-evaluation approach focused on strategic fit, concrete current use cases, workflow impact, integration and security. The principal internal variation is therefore one of emphasis: Moore concentrates on post-purchase usage economics and user capability, while Wilson-Griffin concentrates on pre-purchase evaluation and vendor demonstrations. Both contributions are practitioner observations and advice rather than quantified evidence that the recommended practices improve adoption, quality or renewal outcomes. Although these records are assigned to “Regulators, courts & professional bodies,” the supplied excerpts express Legal Technology Hub advisers’ views; one appears within an episode titled around a judge but is explicitly attributed to Wilson-Griffin. They therefore should not be treated as evidence of a regulatory, judicial or professional-body consensus, nor as representative of that professional voice generally.

qs.q: So now those users are running into high-cost overages on the frontier models in particular, and they’re realizing that low sticker price per month is not their reality, not when their users  don’t know how to use those tools efficiently and how to control cost.

elens.an: The curated 2025 sources collectively support the proposition that rapid legal-AI product expansion and rollout should not be equated with realised organisational value. Their common reasoning is that value depends on practical workflow fit, strategic deployment, user training, change management, knowledge quality, integrations, security, onboarding, sustained support and enforceable governance. Several sources directly distinguish deployment from adoption, while product maps, funding rounds and partnerships are consistently treated as evidence of market activity rather than proof of performance or economic return. Material variation concerns emphasis rather than disagreement: some sources develop structured procurement and agent-oversight criteria; others focus on firms’ internal technical capabilities, platform and database control, or workflow-level pricing. A smaller group redirects attention toward access for smaller firms, vendor education or market consolidation, and several introductory excerpts are too limited to establish a position. Optimistic claims about productivity, agentic adoption and new delivery models are generally forecasts or participant assessments, not measured outcomes. None of the supplied 2025 evidence clearly opposes the proposition, but the corpus is curated and should not be read as representative of all legal-industry participants.

Their common reasoning is that product counts, integrations, launches, token use and licensing show availability or activity, but do not by themselves establish adoption, performance, economic return or sustained use. The more substantive sources therefore emphasise task and workflow fit, organisational readiness, training, cultural change, structured evaluation, renewal review, integration, security, risk-based governance and control over the environment in which lawyers work.
